Meeting header: 
Date: 2026-07-27
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes (recording ended at 15:48)
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Daniel (CTO - Aquila), Maya (CISO), Arjun (Lead ML), Leah (PM)

Summary (auto): 
Quarter-hour intake on data residency, logging dark path and hosting options. Focus on whether Aquila can use Redwood Hosted or needs Dedicated/Private for EU/US data splits and PCI/financial controls. Action items captured at end.

Topics: 
- Hosting models (Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private)
- Data residency and geofencing for EU customers
- Logging retention, redaction and audit trails
- KMS / BYOK and key residency requirements
- HIPAA/PCI-like controls and SOC2 evidence needs
- POC next steps and timelines

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect in places):
[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we got most people on the line, um quick intros — I'm Evan, AE at Redwood inference.
[00:06] Daniel: Hi, Daniel Park, CTO at Aquila Lending. Thanks for doing this.
[00:09] Maya: Maya, CISO. We'll mainly be talking about compliance and where the data flows.
[00:12] Arjun: Arjun, ML lead. I'll dig into latency and model choices.
[00:15] Priya: Priya Nambiar, solutions engineer, I'll take the tech deep dive.
[00:18] Leah: Leah, PM, I'll take notes for the product folks.

[00:35] Evan: Great. The ask you gave us was, uh, to understand whether hosted Redwood API can meet your regulatory obligations, or whether you need Dedicated or our Private offering, right? Can you walk us through your high level constraint?
[00:45] Daniel: Sure. We have EU customers and US customers. For EU accounts we need data in-region, and we have contractual obligations that say PII originating in EU must not be transferred out of EU except under SCCs. For some high-risk loans we also have to retain audit trails for seven years.
[01:05] Maya: Also, from a security control standpoint, we require customer-managed keys for any production secrets and we need to ensure logs don't contain full customer PII. We also need evidence of access controls, RBAC, and audit logs for model calls tied to user IDs.
[01:22] Priya: Okay, good. A couple quick clarifying questions: when you say "logs," do you mean application-level request bodies that might include PII, or do you mean system-level access logs? Sometimes teams have both and treat them differently.
[01:33] Maya: Both. App-level request bodies — like prompt payloads and responses — must be redacted or stored only in-region for EU. System logs we can accept being surfaced to Redwood's control plane if they're redacted, but we need an audit trail showing where they are stored and who accessed them.
[01:48] Evan: Understood. Arjun, can you share your latency SLOs and traffic patterns so we can map hosting options to cost?
[01:54] Arjun: We're doing real-time decisions in the loan flow. P99 latency target is 300-400ms per request, concurrent bursty usage during batch runs overnight. Token counts per request are typically 150–400 tokens.
[02:10] Priya: That's helpful. So tradeoffs: Redwood Hosted gives fastest time to value and our EU regions keep inference in-region, but Hosted logs are stored in our control plane for observability, and historically customers ask for either log redaction or VPC/private options when they need strict residency. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and options to restrict control-plane access; Private (VPC/on-prem) is the most isolated but needs more setup.
[02:32] Maya: How does BYOK work across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private? We have a requirement that keys for production must be customer-managed and can't leave EU. KMS residency is a blocker for Hosted unless you can do a customer-managed KMS in region.
[02:44] Priya: For Hosted we offer an integration with customer KMS using wrapped keys in specific cases, but full BYOK with keys never leaving customer control is only available with Private deployments (VPC or on-prem) where the KMS is in your VPC and Redwood control plane is decoupled. With Dedicated we can offer a hybrid — keys can be in your cloud project in the same region and we support HSM-backed KMS, but the control plane may still surface metrics outside unless we set up region-locked control plane options. I want to call out that, uh, specific enterprise SOWs can add stronger guarantees.
[03:12] Daniel: That hybrid sounds promising. For EU accounts we'd want the model inference and key operations to happen entirely in EU. Do you have a reference architecture for that?
[03:20] Priya: Yes — we have a EU-hosted Dedicated pattern where inference runs in EU GPU pools, the KV cache and prefix caches are kept in-region, and logs can be configured to route to a customer-managed storage account. There's an architecture diagram in our deployment playbook — I'll share the link.
[03:33] Evan: (link note) We'll send the deployment playbook and the SOC2 report after the call.

[03:45] Maya: About logs — can Redwood redact PII automatically before persisting? We need redaction at ingest and not just after.
[03:52] Priya: We have a couple options: automated PII redaction at the prefix/cache layer — it's heuristic-based and fine in many cases but not perfect — or you can front a pre-processing lambda in your VPC that strips PII and only forwards tokens we need for inference. For Private deployments you can require all logs to stay in your environment — our control plane doesn't retain request payloads by default when configured that way.
[04:13] Maya: I hear heuristic. We generally don't accept only heuristics for regulated use-cases. We prefer guaranteed removal.
[04:19] Priya: Totally. If you need guaranteed removal then the Private option with a local preprocessing step is the recommended path. Alternatively we can scope a Dedicated deployment with a strict gateway in region that enforces redaction before it reaches our runtime. That usually ends up in the SOW though.
[04:34] Leah: Quick product question — if we go Dedicated, how much engineering lift is it for Aquila?
[04:38] Priya: For Dedicated it's mostly config and some networking: peering, firewall rules, optional private endpoints. We'll run the deployment and manage the runtime; you manage the VPC side depending on the model. For Private on-prem it's heavier — container images, air-gap checks and your infra team will need to host GPUs.
[04:52] Arjun: For model choices — are there any differences in available models and quantization between Hosted and Dedicated? We rely on smaller quantized models for cost control.
[04:59] Priya: Hosted has the full model catalog and we surface optimized variants. Dedicated supports that catalog as well but some experimental kernels and bleeding-edge quant paths might be staged in Hosted first. For POC we can provision a compatible quantized variant in Dedicated.
[05:13] Daniel: Another regulatory point — we're under some PCI-like constraints for cardholder info during underwriting flows. We need to ensure that any logs with card data never leave our systems and are masked in telemetry. Does Redwood redact tokens at the tokenizer level or do we need to do that?
[05:27] Priya: We don't do tokenizer-level guaranteed redaction that prevents all tokenized storage across the stack in Hosted. You should assume you need to do application-level masking for PCI. For Dedicated/Private you can configure the platform to not persist full request bodies and to mask at the gateway.
[05:41] Maya: What about audit evidence — we need change history and who called what model and when tied to user IDs. Can Redwood provide queryable audit logs and export them to our SIEM (Splunk)?
[05:51] Priya: Yes. We provide audit logs with request metadata, model variant, duration, and user ID if you pass it. We support pushing logs to your Splunk/Datadog via secure forwarding for Dedicated and Private; Hosted can also forward but with more constraints around retention and redaction.
[06:07] Daniel: Okay. On legal — do you sign SCCs and data processing addendums for the Hosted product?
[06:12] Evan: Yes, we have a DPA and can sign SCCs. For higher-assurance controls and region-locking we usually move to Dedicated or Private and include specific clauses in the contract. Our legal team has a template for DPAs and data residency commitments.
[06:24] Maya: For the EU customers, we also have to show evidence of data deletion on request. Do you support deletion flows for stored prompts/embeddings?
[06:33] Priya: We support deletion API for customer-owned storage and for Redwood-managed stored artifacts we have a deletion process — nevertheless for compliance we recommend storing embeddings and long-term artifacts in your own S3 buckets in region and using our connectors so you control deletion.
[06:48] Leah: What about model outputs — are they considered logs or artifacts in Redwood? We sometimes store model responses in our DB for audit and dispute resolution.
[06:56] Priya: Model responses are retained only if configured; default Hosted telemetry retains minimal artifacts but we can configure full response persistence in Dedicated if needed. Again, best practice for regulated output retention is to store in your own system where you control retention policies.
[07:10] Arjun: Regarding performance — do you have any public benchmarks for P99 latency for smaller quantized models on Dedicated? We're trying to hit that 300–400ms target; busy times could see double.
[07:20] Priya: We have an internal perf doc — variances depend on kernel, sequence length, batch size. We'll share sample p99 numbers for a 4-bit quantized 7B model on A100 and T4 variants. For your expected token sizes we think Dedicated with optimized batching will meet p99 in the 200–350ms ballpark. We'll include concrete numbers in the POC runbook.
[07:40] Maya: Another ask — separation of duties: our security team wants to ensure that Redwood operators cannot access customer raw prompts in the EU. Can you describe operator-level access controls?
[07:50] Priya: Operator access is limited, logged, and gated by RBAC. For Hosted, the control plane spans regions and we have internal review processes; for Dedicated we can reduce operator surface and provide more strict access terms in the SOW. Private deployments eliminate Redwood operator access to customer data when fully air-gapped.
[08:06] Daniel: Sounds like we need to map which flows can remain Hosted and which must be Private. Practically, what do customers do — split traffic?
[08:14] Evan: Many customers partition by dataset or endpoint: low-risk requests on Hosted, high-risk EU or PCI-sensitive flows on Dedicated or Private. We also support smart routing by policy — route by tenant or endpoint to different deployment pools.
[08:27] Leah: That would be ideal for our rollout. Pilot low-risk features in Hosted and move underwriting flows to Dedicated.

[08:40] (short silence, then side conversation)
[08:45] Maya: On the topic of keys, if we use Dedicated with customer KMS in EU, can Redwood sign encryption keys that never leave the EU?
[08:53] Priya: Yes, with Dedicated we can configure keywrap where the master key resides in your EU KMS and only wrapped keys are used by Redwood runtime in-region. The unwrap operations happen inside EU infrastructure. For Hosted that level of residency is harder but sometimes doable with special enterprise contracts.
[09:10] Arjun: How about storage of KV caches and embeddings — are they encrypted at rest and can they be kept in customer-managed storage?
[09:17] Priya: KV caches are encrypted at rest. We can also integrate with customer-managed storage for blobs and embeddings so that you control encryption and residency. We'll note that embedding indexing might still require temporary compute in-region.
[09:30] Daniel: What kind of SLA can we expect for Dedicated? We need predictable throughput for underwriting workflows.
[09:36] Evan: Dedicated comes with SLA options in the enterprise plan. We guarantee uptime SLAs and throughput baselines, and we can include burst capacity in the SOW.

[09:50] Maya: One more — we need a list of compliance certifications and third-party audit reports.
[09:54] Evan: We'll send SOC2 Type II report, and we also have ISO docs available on request. For HIPAA-specific language we can provide a BA agreement for private deployments.
[10:04] (overlap) Maya: BAAs? Yes, that's required for health adjacent data.
[10:08] Priya: For HIPAA you'll want Private or Dedicated configured with minimal operator access. We'll escalate to our compliance team for BAAs.

[10:18] Evan: Ok, to recap the high level — Aquila's constraints: EU in-region processing, customer-managed keys for production, guaranteed PII deletion, seven-year retention for certain artifacts, and queryable audit logs. Recommended path: pilot low-risk workloads on Hosted (EU region) while running a Dedicated/Private POC for underwriting and PCI-like flows.
[10:40] Daniel: That matches our mental model. Next practical steps?
[10:44] Evan: We'll send the SOC2, DPA, deployment playbook, and a POC runbook that outlines tests for latency, log retention, and redaction. We'll propose a POC week of 2026-08-10.
[10:55] Maya: We'll share our compliance matrix and list of endpoints that must remain in EU by 2026-08-03.
[11:01] Evan: Great. Priya, any final technical notes?
[11:04] Priya: I'll include detailed architecture diagrams for the EU Dedicated pattern, sample log-forwarding config for Splunk, and sample KMS keywrap setup. Also I'll include perf numbers and expected token costs.
[11:15] Leah: Perfect. We'll review and follow up with legal and infra.

[11:24] (closing)
[11:25] Evan: Thanks everyone, we'll circulate notes and the links. If anything changes please ping me.
[11:30] Daniel: Thanks, Evan.
[11:32] Maya: Thanks.
